reason: The sources provide multi-site verified receipts detailing Rosetta's 31-month deep-space hibernation, wake-up, comet orbit, and surface landing.
story: In 2004, the European Space Agency launched Rosetta on a ten-year voyage to rendezvous with Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. By June 2011, as the solar-powered probe drifted near Jupiter's orbit nearly 800 million kilometers from the Sun, sunlight grew too weak to keep its systems alive. Mission controllers commanded Rosetta to shut down almost everything: instruments, radio transmitters, and reaction wheels. For 31 months, the probe drifted in frozen, radio-silent hibernation. The only thing running was an internal clock ticking away in deep space. On January 20, 2014, that pre-programmed alarm clock went off. Hundreds of millions of kilometers away, Rosetta thawed its thrusters, reoriented itself, pointed its main antenna toward Earth, and beamed back a signal: 'Hello, world!' Rosetta went on to make history as the first probe to orbit a comet, deployed the Philae lander, and concluded its mission by softly landing on the comet in 2016.
angle: To survive near Jupiter's orbit on solar power alone, the Rosetta spacecraft turned off all systems and drifted frozen in radio silence for 31 months until an internal alarm clock woke it up.

claims.claim: Rosetta was a space mission developed and spearheaded by the European Space Agency (ESA).
Rosetta launched on 2 March 2004 from Kourou, French Guiana, aboard an Ariane 5 rocket.
The total cost of the Rosetta mission was approximately 1.3 billion euros.
To gain sufficient speed, Rosetta completed four planetary gravity assists: three flybys of Earth and one of Mars.
During its interplanetary cruise, Rosetta conducted flybys of asteroids 2867 Šteins and 21 Lutetia.
Rosetta was powered primarily by solar cells rather than nuclear power.
In June 2011, mission controllers placed Rosetta into deep-space hibernation as it traveled far from the Sun.
Rosetta's deep-space hibernation lasted for 31 months.
On 20 January 2014, Rosetta successfully exited hibernation and restored radio communications with Earth.
Rosetta's post-hibernation wake-up signal was received on Earth at NASA's Goldstone ground station.
Upon its successful wake-up in January 2014, the mission greeted the world with the message 'Hello, world!'.
Rosetta rendezvoused with Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko in August 2014 after a 10-year cruise.
Rosetta became the first spacecraft in history to enter orbit around a comet nucleus.
Close-up imaging revealed that Comet 67P consists of a double-lobed shape resembling a rubber duck.
Rosetta carried a 100-kilogram lander module named Philae.
On 12 November 2014, Philae made the first soft landing on a comet's surface.
Upon touchdown, Philae bounced twice across the comet's surface before coming to a stop.
Rosetta was the first spacecraft to escort and follow a comet as it swung around the Sun.
Rosetta's instruments detected free molecular oxygen gas surrounding the comet nucleus.
The mission was controlled from the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany.
On 30 September 2016, Rosetta concluded its mission with a controlled impact onto the comet's surface.
Rosetta's final descent targeted the Ma'at region on Comet 67P.
Rosetta's impact speed onto the comet surface was approximately walking speed, or 2 miles per hour (3.2 km/h).
Holger Sierks served as the principal investigator for Rosetta's OSIRIS imaging camera system.

disputed: Origin of Earth's water from comets: S2 states that in December 2014, ROSINA found 67P's water had more than three times the heavy water ratio of Earth's water, arguing against cometary delivery, whereas S1 reports a 2024 re-analysis corrected a measurement error and showed 67P's isotopic composition actually matches Earth's. Script should attribute this as an initial 2014 finding that was revised by a 2024 re-analysis.

Philae planned landing date: S4 lists the planned landing date as 11 November 2014, whereas S1 and S2 record the actual landing on 12 November 2014. Script should treat 11 November as an early target date and 12 November as the actual landing date.
Mission cost conversion: S1 cites €1.3 billion as US$1.8 billion, while S6 cites €1.3 billion as US$1.46 billion due to currency fluctuations. Script should state the original €1.3 billion figure.
